video_title: The $300 Billion Stablecoin War Has Begun with Christian Schmid, Alexander Paddington & Sergio Mello
gist: BCG partners (banking/transaction banking) and Anchorage Digital's head of stablecoin solutions argue that after the GENIUS Act, banks must run stablecoins and tokenized deposits in parallel, that distribution/network effect (not the token) decides winners, and that the real prize is balance-sheet/liquidity efficiency and ecosystem reach rather than reserve yield. The Clarity Act's failed Senate vote (the day before recording) delays rewards/yield rules and on-chain trading growth but, per the panel, not cross-border, treasury or correspondent-banking adoption.

themes.theme: Bank consortia vs. Tether/Circle: distribution wins

insights.claim: A consortium of 21 banks, including some of the largest US banks, announced a joint stablecoin roughly two weeks before the recording; the stated rationale is that a single bank cannot generate enough liquidity for its own coin, whereas pooled distribution networks create credible competition to Tether and Circle.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid (BCG)
insights.so_what: Single-bank stablecoins are likely to struggle on liquidity; watch consortium coins (US 21-bank, EU Qivalis) as the real challengers to USDT/USDC share.
insights.quote: a single bank alone it's tough to create liquidity because it's only a single bank so if banks kind of join together use their distribution network you can create a much more credible competition to tether and circle

insights.claim: A bank-issued stablecoin is effectively a payment network, not a branded token, so its real competitors are other settlement networks rather than other tokens; banks should study how Zelle/Early Warning Services and The Clearing House were built as banking consortia.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Evaluate bank stablecoin efforts on acceptance/critical-mass metrics like a payment network, not on token issuance headlines.
insights.quote: the real competitors to an institutional bankdriven consortium driven stable coin is other settlement networks more than other tokens

insights.claim: Tether's success came from a decade of grassroots distribution in the Global South and emerging markets, filling a utility gap for dollar accounts with hundreds of millions of active users; stablecoin success depends on reaching critical mass of acceptance quickly.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Tether's EM retail moat is hard to attack head-on; bank coins need distinct use cases rather than competing in Tether's core market.

insights.claim: Lessons from co-founding the Global Dollar Network (with Kraken, Robinhood and a third firm captioned 'Axus'): setting up the right use cases with local utility and liquidity from day one matters far more than marketing or secondary-market liquidity; Anchorage later stepped back to focus on the issuance layer to avoid competing with its issuer clients on distribution.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Discount stablecoin launches promoted via exchange listings/marketing; favor those with captive day-one settlement flows.

insights.claim: Distribution outcomes are binary because of network effects: a stablecoin either reaches a localized critical mass that sets off a chain reaction or it achieves nothing; governance is the hardest part for consortia.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Expect a winner-take-most dynamic and many failed launches; consortium governance friction is a key execution risk.
insights.quote: It's really a binary a binary outcome. You either nail it or you don't because it's a network effect success.

insights.claim: Launch timelines differ sharply: a solo issuer can work on a 30/60/90-day plan, but with multiple parties in governance it becomes more like 90/180/365 days, though consortia start with bigger reach; sequence is chain/signing/wallet choices, then legal and reserve-management decisions, then distribution strategy.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Consortium coins announced now likely won't have meaningful live volume for roughly a year.

insights.claim: Tether and Circle hold about 85% of the stablecoin market, but the panel argues the past is nearly irrelevant because the addressable market is the tens-of-trillions M2 money supply yet to be tokenized; banks should target capturing $100-500 billion of it.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Incumbent share may persist in crypto/EM while banks grow a separate, potentially larger tokenized-M2 pool; total stablecoin/tokenized money supply could expand far beyond $300B.
insights.quote: whatever happened in the past 10 years is almost irrelevant

insights.claim: Distribution will decide the stablecoin game and the market will not stay a two-player duopoly; many issuers will reach scale, though it will take time.
insights.speaker: Alexander Paddington (BCG)
insights.so_what: Watch for share erosion of the top two over a multi-year horizon as bank and non-bank coins gain distribution.
insights.quote: I think ultimately distribution will be what wins the game and I don't think only two will be at scale

insights.claim: The signing of the GENIUS Act in July 2025 was the inflection point at which bank stablecoin conversations turned into procurement processes, with meetings moving from innovation/digital-asset teams to legal, compliance and treasury.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Bank stablecoin adoption is past the pilot stage; infra vendors (custody, issuance-as-a-service) should see real contracts.
insights.quote: That that's where all the conversations became uh procurement processes.

insights.claim: The Clarity Act failed its Senate vote the day before recording; the panel expects it to delay rules on stablecoin rewards and amendments to GENIUS, possibly beyond this year, but not to slow institutional adoption, citing US Bank launching its own stablecoin the prior week.
insights.speaker: Alexander Paddington (BCG)
insights.so_what: Treat the Clarity setback as a timing issue for rewards/market-structure rules, not a halt to bank stablecoin launches.
insights.quote: this might not be this year

insights.claim: The Clarity Act delay mainly hurts stablecoin growth as the cash leg of on-chain trading by financial institutions; cross-border, treasury management, payments and correspondent dollar clearing do not need to wait for it.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Regulatory delay is a bigger headwind for tokenized securities/on-chain trading volumes than for payments-oriented stablecoin use.
insights.quote: stable coins are effectively cash lag for the onchain economy

insights.claim: Community banks and large banks took a joint position against Clarity Act provisions seen as loopholes allowing interest-like stablecoin rewards; GENIUS prohibits payment-stablecoin yield, and community banks claim rewards could drain $1.3 trillion of deposits.
insights.speaker: Alexander Paddington (BCG)
insights.so_what: The rewards/yield question is the core battleground; its resolution determines deposit flight risk for banks and economics for exchanges paying rewards.

insights.claim: Regulators are moving in favor of stablecoins as multifaceted tools: some are allowing equivalent capital and LCR liquidity treatment, accounting standards are adapting, and the CFTC issued statements on stablecoin collateral with haircuts of only 2%.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Low collateral haircuts and favorable capital/liquidity treatment make stablecoins usable as margin and balance-sheet assets, expanding institutional demand.
insights.quote: CFTC uh issued uh statements also about collateral and and haircuts there of only 2%

insights.claim: Regulatory clarity will always lag technology, so banks should plan 12-18 months ahead and expect regulation to catch up by launch rather than waiting for full clarity.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Banks that wait for final rules will be 12-18 months behind; first movers gain network position.
insights.quote: you always have to think 12 18 months ahead and expect regulation to catch up

insights.claim: A US CBDC is unlikely soon given the clear push against it; momentum is behind private forms of digital money (stablecoins and tokenized deposits), while the digital euro remains a focus elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Alexander Paddington (BCG)
insights.so_what: US digital-dollar upside accrues to private issuers and banks rather than the Fed.

insights.claim: Stablecoins and tokenized deposits are not either/or: stablecoins have network reach and interoperability and fit retail and crypto use cases, while tokenized deposits (live at over a dozen banks, so far within each bank's own four walls) fit multinational corporates; consortium work (e.g., in the UK) aims to make tokenized deposits interoperable.
insights.speaker: Alexander Paddington (BCG)
insights.so_what: Banks need to play both; tokenized deposits' scale depends on cross-bank interoperability efforts.
insights.quote: What's clear is you you can't you know choose one. You you do need to actually play both

insights.claim: Tokenized deposits are eligible collateral for stablecoin reserves, so stablecoin growth feeds deposit and tokenized-deposit growth and vice versa; where an institution draws its 'four walls' line between tokenized deposit (inside) and stablecoin (outside) is a fundamental design choice.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Counters the deposit-drain narrative: banks can capture stablecoin reserve balances as deposits.
insights.quote: tokenized deposits are a form of eligible collateral for stable coin reserves

insights.claim: Early stablecoins backed reserves mostly with money market funds and Treasuries, but the next generation will distribute reserves more through the banking system as deposits, giving banks reserve-related revenue.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: A shift of reserve composition from T-bills/MMFs toward bank deposits would affect front-end Treasury demand and benefit reserve-holding banks.
insights.quote: The earlier stable coins were mostly using MMFs, money market funds and treasuries as a as a mechanism for reserves. But the next generation will be a lot more distributed through the financial system.

insights.claim: For 2027, stablecoins will be the bigger story by volume but tokenized deposits by consequence, since every bank's deposits will eventually be tokenized.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Stablecoin volume headlines will dominate near term; structural change to bank balance sheets comes via tokenized deposits.
insights.quote: stable coins by volume but tokenized deposits by consequence

insights.claim: Anchorage is the largest custodian of a tokenized fund captioned 'bido' (likely BUIDL) and of two tokenized money market funds from JPMorgan and others; the market is small but users report large efficiency gains.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Tokenized MMFs are an early but growing institutional cash product; custody concentration at Anchorage is notable.

themes.theme: Use cases: what's real, overrated, underrated

insights.claim: The highest-value tokenized-money use cases for corporates are 24/7 real-time cross-border payments (avoiding cut-offs and multi-hop correspondent chains), treasury automation via smart contracts, and later on-chain FX; value is greatest for multinationals with intraday liquidity volatility across time zones.
insights.speaker: Alexander Paddington (BCG)
insights.so_what: Target cross-border and multinational treasury flows when sizing stablecoin/tokenized deposit adoption.

insights.claim: Domestic stablecoin payments are the most overrated use case because domestic rails (RTP in the US, and equivalents intra-Europe and in Brazil) are already efficient.
insights.speaker: Alexander Paddington (BCG)
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of stablecoin payment plays premised on domestic P2P/merchant payments in markets with instant rails.
insights.quote: there's a lot of hype about domestic um payments for stable coins

insights.claim: Correspondent banking is the most underrated stablecoin use case; Anchorage launched a stablecoin correspondent banking program offering a nostro/vostro account in both fiat and stablecoins with 24/7/365 mobility and minimal balance requirements.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Correspondent banking is a huge legacy construct; stablecoin-enabled nostro accounts threaten trapped-liquidity models of incumbents.

insights.claim: Stablecoin-backed cards are an exciting, real and fast-growing use case, cited with Visa/Mastercard published data and a neobank's (captioned 'new bank', likely Nubank) multicurrency stablecoin accounts with attached cards.
insights.speaker: Alexander Paddington (BCG)
insights.so_what: Card networks and neobanks are early beneficiaries of stablecoin spending flows.

themes.theme: Where banks make money and the cost of waiting

insights.claim: The biggest monetization opportunity for banks is balance-sheet efficiency: freeing trapped cash held across entities and jurisdictions for intraday and end-of-day liquidity buffers, beyond custody fees on reserves and transaction-fee savings.
insights.speaker: Alexander Paddington (BCG)
insights.so_what: The return case is lower liquidity buffers and capital, not fee revenue; watch for banks citing liquidity savings.
insights.quote: I think the biggest opportunity that that I'm excited about is the balance sheet efficiency

insights.claim: For banks the value is ecosystem capture rather than short-term yield: a stablecoin that interoperates with tokenized deposits extends the bank's services beyond its four walls to users otherwise locked out.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Judge bank stablecoin programs by customer reach gained, not reserve income.
insights.quote: I think the money is more in the ecosystem capture more than the short-term yield

insights.claim: If Treasury yields plummet, the reserve-income component of stablecoins becomes less appealing, but the settlement-network and payment utility remain, so network-effect stablecoins stay useful regardless of yield.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Issuer economics (e.g., Circle/Tether) are rate-sensitive even if usage is not; falling rates compress issuer revenue.

insights.claim: Double-digit numbers of systemically important banks are already live in production with real digital-asset use cases, and most others are in pilots or consortia; serving digital-asset firms (payments, custodians, trading) as their bank is a large growing market, and not participating carries major opportunity cost.
insights.speaker: Alexander Paddington (BCG)
insights.so_what: Banking crypto firms is a growth niche; laggard banks risk losing that client segment.

insights.claim: Not participating in stablecoin networks carries the same danger as a bank that declined to join SWIFT decades ago.
insights.speaker: Sergio Mello (Anchorage Digital)
insights.so_what: Frames stablecoin networks as future core interbank utilities; holdouts face exclusion.
insights.quote: It's the same danger that a bank would have not joining swift 20 50 years ago.
